title: The 30% your platform never shipped
description: Every ERP covers roughly seventy per cent of what a business needs. The rest is systems engineering, and it is where the money goes.
content:
Ask any implementation partner what a platform covers out of the box and you will get roughly the same number: seventy per cent. The remaining thirty is configuration, integration, reporting and exception handling — and it is where the second, larger budget goes.

Why it never closes

The thirty per cent is not a backlog. It is the shape of the business: the entity structure, the approval matrix, the way this company recognises revenue, the four exceptions the finance team carries in their heads. A vendor cannot ship it because it is not general.

What changed

What changed is not that AI can now write the configuration. It is that it can operate the systems: log in, read the record, apply the rule, execute, and leave a trail an auditor accepts. The thirty per cent stops being a project and becomes a run.

title: An agent that reads is a report. An agent that writes is a colleague
description: Read-only agents are safe, useful and stop exactly where the work begins. Here is how we made writing safe instead.
content:
Almost every enterprise AI deployment stops at read. It is the responsible place to stop, and it is also the place where the value stops.

Four properties

A write is safe when it is scoped, reversible, attributable and approved. Anvil will not perform one unless all four hold.

  • Scoped — the service account can touch the objects the run declares and nothing else
  • Reversible — every write is posted as a batch that can be reversed as a batch
  • Attributable — the ledger records the rule, the inputs and the version of both
  • Approved — a named human holds the last step

The uncomfortable part

Approval is a queue, and queues rot. So the approval is small: one screen, the diff, the rule, the exception. If approving takes longer than doing it by hand, nobody will, and the agent is worthless.

title: Two weeks, not two quarters
description: What actually happens in the fourteen days between signing and the first live run.
content:
Enterprise software is sold in quarters because it is implemented in quarters. Ours is not, and the reason is unglamorous: we do not ask you to change anything.

Week one

We connect to a sandbox copy of your tenant with a read-only service account and run against a period you have already closed. You compare our ledger to what your team actually did. This is the week where we are wrong in front of you.

Week two

The run goes live in parallel. It proposes; your team disposes. At the end of the week you decide which steps it may execute directly and which stay proposal-only. Most customers start with two.

After

A new run every quarter, chosen by whichever workflow is costing you the most hands.

title: The ledger is the product
description: We spent longer on the record of what the agent did than on the agent.
content:
The first version of Anvil had a chat interface and a spinner. It worked, and nobody trusted it, because nobody could see what it had done.

What we built instead

One append-only ledger. Every read, every decision, every write, with the rule version and the approver. It is the first screen, not a settings page, and it is the thing customers show their auditors.

The agent is replaceable. Models change every few months. The record of what happened in your systems is not.
